$comment: The values this repository is willing to pass for arguments the inventory cannot give a
domain to, plus the arguments it refuses to vary and why.
Paths point inside the oracle container, where MakeFixtures.java writes the corpus. They are
not committed files: the corpus is rebuilt from the program on every run, which keeps it
deterministic and keeps binary fixtures out of the tree.
Adding a value here widens a covering array. Adding an exclusion narrows it, and the reason
is required, because an exclusion is the one thing in this file that can hide a difference.
There is no constraint forbidding a block-compressed input with a `.idx` output. The reference
REFUSES that pair by name, and a refusal is behaviour a port has to reproduce, so the row is
kept and both sides are compared on the refusal rather than on an output.
`--bgzf-file` takes a block-compressed file and a plain one: the second is a refusal the
reference makes by name, and a row that reproduces a refusal is as much of the claim as a row
that reproduces a report.
`--input` carries the BAM as well as the three feature files: it is one argument name on two
kinds of tool, and a read walker refuses a VCF the way IndexFeatureFile refuses a BAM, so both
refusals are rows rather than exclusions.
`--variant` takes an INDEXED VCF and an unindexed one. A feature walker refuses `-L` against
an input with no random access, so a list with only the unindexed file would compare two
refusals on every interval row and never reach a traversal; and dropping the unindexed one
would lose that refusal, which is behaviour too.
`CountVariants` overrides `--output`: the shared list is an index's name, and this tool writes
a count. A `.idx` there would measure nothing but a file name.
`--use-jdk-deflater` used to be excluded here, on the ground that these tools write nothing
compressed. That stopped being true when IndexFeatureFile learned to write a tabix index: a
.tbi is a BGZF file, and the deflater decides its bytes. The argument is a boolean with a
domain of its own, so it needs no fixture; what it needed was for the exclusion to be read
again after the tool changed.
`--reference` takes two FASTAs, each with the .fai and .dict beside it that GATK requires: one
on the corpus's own contig and one on a contig it does not carry. The reference dictionary
takes part in the validation and outranks the reads' in the best-available chain, so the
second value is a refusal and the first is not.
`GatherVcfsCloud` holds `--create-output-variant-index` at FALSE, and the reason is the
measurement rather than the port. A Tribble index records the last-modified time of the file
it indexes, and here that file is the tool's own OUTPUT: the two sides write their own copy at
their own moment, so the two indexes differ in eight bytes of clock and the row measures when
the run happened. The port builds the index byte for byte otherwise -- checked against the
reference's own on one input -- and every other tool indexes a file both sides were GIVEN.
`--read-index` takes two paths that both exist, because what the argument decides is not
whether the file is there: an index handed to an input that is neither a BAM nor a CRAM is
refused by htsjdk's text-SAM branch whatever it contains, and the count is checked against the
number of reads inputs before the contents are read at all.
`--sequence-dictionary` takes two: one that agrees with the corpus's contig and one that
shares nothing with it. The MASTER dictionary is validated against every other one before the
traversal, so the second value is a refusal and the first is not, and both are behaviour.
Four arguments are here with a SECOND value and no expectation that they change anything:
`--tmp-dir`, the two cloud prefetch buffers and `--seconds-between-progress-updates`. Each was
excluded as having one value, which meant the array covered it by holding it at its default
and could not have noticed if it mattered. A row that varies them and gets the same answer on
both sides is a claim; a row that never varied them was not.
`--exclude-intervals` and the two paddings are here because the four arguments beside `-L` in
IntervalArgumentCollection had no domain at all: an int with only its default is excluded as
having one value, and a free-form string with no default is excluded for having none. With no
values they were covered by being absent, which is the one setting that cannot disagree.
The three read-filter arguments are here for the same reason. `--inverted-read-filter` names
filters that are neither a tool default nor a value of `--read-filter`: inverting a default is
refused outright, and inverting a filter the same row enables is refused too, so an overlap
would spend rows on refusals the unit suite already covers. And
`--disable-read-filter` names WellformedReadFilter, which IS the default, so the row actually
removes a filter rather than warning about one that was never there. Both take a second value
because one is no domain at all: an argument with a single value is covered by being present
or absent, which the generator excludes for the same reason it excludes a lone default.
$per_tool: A tool whose `--INPUT` is not the kind of file the shared value names declares its own here,
as `"per_tool": { "<Tool>": { "--INPUT": [...] } }`. The override replaces the shared list
`CreateHadoopBamSplittingIndex` declares its own `--input` and `--output`: the shared input
list carries three feature files this tool refuses by EXTENSION before it opens anything, so
an array built from it would measure one refusal four times. Two values are enough to have the
refusal and the index both.
It takes TWO names for the same reason every other argument here does: one value is covered by
being present or absent, and the second is what lets a row notice that the tool writes where it
was told to.
for that tool only. This repository has no such tool yet; picard-rs does, and the mechanism
lives here because the generator does.
See tools/coverage/README.md.
`reads2.bam` is the second BAM, and the reason it exists is that an argument with ONE fixture
value is held at it: the row carries it, no row varies it, and nothing can notice whether it
matters. Every read-taking tool therefore names two BAMs. They differ in the three ways the
corpus needs: a different record count, positions on the other side of both interval fixtures,
and two records the default read filters disagree about (a leading-deletion cigar that
`GoodCigarReadFilter` refuses, and an unmapped record that `MappedReadFilter` removes).
`recal2.table` and `reads2.bai` follow it, so `--bqsr-recal-file` and `--read-index` have a
value that belongs to the input in the row and a value that belongs to the other one.
The read tools name their own `--intervals` as well, and the reason is `distinct_outputs`
rather than acceptance: the shared `chr1:1-1000` holds two of the first BAM's reads and the
exclusion fixture removes one of them, so every accepted row answered 0 or 1 and an array of
twenty rows observed two outputs. `chr1:1-6000` spans all eight reads of `reads.bam` and three
of `reads2.bam`, and `chr1:50000-60000` spans none of the first and two of the second, which is
what makes a padding, an exclusion or a read filter visible as a different number.
`CountVariants` names its own `--input` for a reason the other tools do not have: it is a
VARIANT walker, so `--input` is the optional READS beside the driving variants, and the shared
list carries three feature files. A row that pairs one of those with a `--read-index` is
refused by htsjdk before the tool runs (`Cannot use index file with textual SAM file`), which
was fourteen of its thirty-one rows measuring one refusal. Two BAMs and the indexes that belong
to them turn those rows into traversals whose reads dictionary is compared against the
features', which is what the tool actually does with them.
`CountBases` and `FlagStat` take `CountReads`' values verbatim, which is the archetype paying
for itself: the three declare the same seventy arguments and read the same files, so the
fixtures that made one measurable make all three.
`CountBasesInReference` names the two BAMs even though a reference walker never opens them:
the standard read arguments are its inheritance, so a row pairing a `--read-index` with the
shared list's feature files is refused by htsjdk before the tool runs, and eleven of its
twenty-three rows measured that one refusal. It names the read walkers' intervals for the
same reason the others do: the corpus's reference carries the same contig.
`SplitIntervals` writes a DIRECTORY, so its `--output` values are two directory names the run
creates rather than two files. Its own five arguments carry two values each: a scatter count
of one and of three, a minimum contig size that keeps both contigs and one that drops the
second, and the two halves of a file name.
`--interval-file-prefix` carries two NON-EMPTY names, and the tool's own default is the empty
string: a covering array writes every argument as `--name value`, so an empty value leaves the
next token to be read as a positional argument and the row is refused before the tool runs.
`Pileup` takes the read walkers' corpus because it IS a read walker's startup with a different
traversal after it. `PreprocessIntervals` opens no reads and still DECLARES them, so it takes
the two BAMs for the same reason `CountBasesInReference` does: a row pairing a `--read-index`
with the shared list's feature files is refused by htsjdk before the tool runs. Its own two
arguments, `--bin-length` and `--padding`, are what decide the bins it writes.
`IllegalArgumentException`s: the merging rule must be OVERLAPPING_ONLY and the interval padding
must be zero, because the tool bins and pads by its own `--bin-length` and `--padding` instead.
Each is held at the one value the tool accepts; varying them measured that refusal on nine of
twenty-one rows and nothing else.
`PreprocessIntervals` refuses FOUR of the standard interval arguments in its own
`IllegalArgumentException`s -- the set rule must be UNION, the exclusion padding and the
interval padding must be zero, and the merging rule must be OVERLAPPING_ONLY -- because it bins
reproduces each refusal, so a row that carries one measures behaviour rather than a gap.
and each is HELD at the value the tool accepts. Varying them measured the refusal on twenty of
twenty-one rows and left ONE distinct output, which is an array that covers its arguments
without testing them; held, the same array runs nine accepted rows over four outputs. The
refusals are the runner's and are reproduced -- they are simply not what these rows spend
themselves on.
`PrintDistantMates` and `GetSampleName` take the read walkers' corpus unchanged, which is what
the archetype is for: the first writes a BAM like `PrintReads` and the second reads a header
and nothing else, and both open the same files by the same arguments.
`PrintDistantMates` names `pairs.bam` first, and it is the only tool that needs it: every
record's mate is read, and the other BAMs are unpaired, so the REFERENCE answered `Cannot get
mate information for an unpaired read` on eight of its rows. The second value is one of those
unpaired BAMs, which keeps that refusal in the array rather than losing it.
`CompareIntervalLists` names `--L` and `--L2`, which are ITS OWN scalars rather than the
engine's interval collection: two values each, so the array sees the same list compared with
itself and a shorter one compared with a longer, which are the three verdicts the tool has.
`CompareIntervalLists` writes NO FILE: its verdict is a line on standard output or an
exception, and the corpus records the output files plus the first error line. So its accepted
rows all read as the empty output and `distinct_outputs` is 1 by construction rather than for
want of fixtures -- what the array measures for this tool is which of the three verdicts each
row reaches, and two of them are exceptions the corpus does record.
`AnnotateIntervals` holds the same four interval arguments `PreprocessIntervals` holds, and for
the same reason: both call `validateIntervalArgumentCollection`, and varying them measures that
refusal instead of the table the tool writes.
`CheckPileup` takes `Pileup`'s corpus -- one locus walker's startup is the other's -- plus the
two mpileup files it compares against: `truth.pileup` is the REFERENCE's own `Pileup` output
converted to samtools' six columns, so it agrees with the traversal at every locus, and
`wrong.pileup` disagrees at the first, which is the difference between a run that validates and
a run that is refused.
It HOLDS `--max-depth-per-sample` at zero, which is the one hold in this file that names a gap
in the port rather than a refusal in the tool: any value above zero asks for the locus
iterator's leveling downsampler, which the port does not carry, so the row would compare a
traversal against the port's own limitation message. `Pileup` varies the same argument and
measures nothing by it -- every one of its rows carrying two is refused earlier, for a
dictionary the reads do not match -- so the argument has never actually been measured here.
gatk-rs#1102 is the downsampler; when it lands both tools can vary this again.
`FastaReferenceMaker` takes `CountBasesInReference`'s corpus, which is the reference walker's:
the reads it declares are never opened and are there so that a `--read-index` paired with a
feature file is refused by htsjdk rather than measured. Its own `--line-width` carries the
writer's default and a width narrow enough to wrap the corpus's intervals more than once, which
is what makes the argument visible in the FASTA rather than only present.
`GetPileupSummaries` needs a POPULATION vcf, which the corpus did not have: the tool refuses a
file whose header declares no `AF` before its first locus, so an array built on `reads.vcf`
would have measured that one refusal on every row. `population.vcf` carries the field and sits
on the reads of `reads.bam`, one record per read, with frequencies straddling the default
window and a triallelic site the tool skips whatever its frequency is. `indexed.vcf` is the
second value, which keeps the header refusal in the array rather than losing it. It holds
`--max-depth-per-sample` at zero for the same reason `CheckPileup` does (gatk-rs#1102).
`CalculateContamination` reads the table `GetPileupSummaries` writes, and the corpus therefore
carries two of those tables produced by the REFERENCE itself rather than written by hand: the
chain is the point, so the second tool is measured on a table the first really writes. The
second table, over `reads2.bam`, is what gives `--matched-normal` a value that is not the
input, which is the argument that decides whether the genotyping model is rebuilt.
`PrintReadsHeader` takes the read walkers' corpus unchanged: it opens the reads for their
header and asks for no record.
`UnmarkDuplicates` takes the read walkers' corpus unchanged: it writes a BAM like `PrintReads`
and differs from it only in the flag bit it clears.
`CollectReadCounts` HOLDS `--format` at TSV, and that is the second hold naming a gap in the
port rather than a refusal in the tool: the tool's own default is HDF5, which is a file format
this port does not write at all (gatk-rs#1107). It holds the same four interval arguments
`PreprocessIntervals` and `AnnotateIntervals` hold, for the same reason and by the same
`validateIntervalArgumentCollection`.

$why: deep.bam is the only file in this corpus with a stack deep enough for --max-depth-per-sample to
thin: eight reads at 1005 and four at 1105, each with a different base, so a thinned column is
visible in the output rather than merely smaller. reads.bam beside it has a depth of one.
--max-variants-per-shard is held at 0, for the reason CallableLoci holds it: its other value is
refused by the parser and a locus walker never reads it.
The constraints below are what make the thinning observable at all (#1135). A t=2 array
guarantees the pair (deep.bam, target 2) appears once; it does not guarantee that the row it
lands on runs, and the first measurement put it on a row whose dictionary makes the interval
invalid. The clauses keep the maskers off the rows that carry a target above zero.
--max-depth-per-sample is no longer held at zero: the locus iterator's reservoir and leveling
thin -- eight reads at one locus, where every other file here has a depth of one.
--max-depth-per-sample is no longer held at zero: the locus iterator's downsamplers are wired
in (#1102), so the argument is a value like any other here. Its DEPTH is measured on `Pileup`,
whose input can be deep.bam; this tool's is the file its truth pileup was built from, and a
pileup compared against a truth file for a different input measures the pairing rather than
the tool.
The other half of the chain: --mixing-fractions takes the table CalculateMixingFractions
wrote over duo.vcf, produced by the REFERENCE in the corpus build, and a table naming a
sample the VCF does not have. The second value is this tool's NullPointerException, which
is what a missing sample really produces: the fractions are looked up by name into a map
and the miss is unboxed.
--variant carries duo.vcf, whose two samples are what the annotation multiplies, and
reads.vcf, which declares no sample at all.
--read-index and --input are held out: this tool reads no reads.
duo.vcf and reads.vcf for the variants, and the corpus's two BAMs for the depth. What this
tool counts is CONTAINMENT of the record's whole span rather than overlap, so a record at a
read's last base counts nothing and one inside it counts one.
--add-output-vcf-command-line is held at FALSE, and the reason is this tool's own rather
than the shared one: its default header lines DO reach the file, unlike its sibling's, and
the ##GATKCommandLine line carries the run's own wall-clock time.
--create-output-variant-index is held at FALSE for the reason every variant writer holds
it: the index records the output file's last-modified time.
shifted.vcf against population.vcf, and indexed.vcf against itself. shifted.vcf is the
population VCF with every allele frequency moved, and moved by DIFFERENT amounts: a file
compared with itself has a delta of zero at every true positive, so the mean and the
standard deviation are zero whatever the arithmetic does, and a constant offset would
leave the deviation zero as well. The first measurement was exactly that, two distinct
outputs over eight accepted rows.
identity case: every record is a true positive and every difference is zero, which is the
row that says the walk and the arithmetic agree. The second shares no INFO key, and the
refusal that produces is the check onTraversalStart makes against the HEADERS.
--eval-info-key and --truth-info-key carry AF, which population.vcf declares, and a key no
header declares. A key the header declares and no record carries would be a third case, and
the tool's own suite has it.
--input and --read-index are held out: this tool reads no reads.
segments.cr.seg is the corpus's copy-ratio segment file, written by hand because
ModelSegments would need read counts and allelic counts this corpus does not carry. Its
five segments straddle the copy-neutral window, so the calls are 0, - and + rather than one
letter repeated.
The four bounds and thresholds are what this tool is: the neutral window decides which
segments the statistics are computed over, and the two z-score thresholds decide the
outliers and the calls. Each carries its default and a value that moves the answer, and one
of the lower bounds is NEGATIVE, which is the IllegalArgumentException the caller raises
before it looks at a segment.
indexed.vcf and population.vcf: the first has a sample and a GT, the second an INFO field
and no genotype column at all, so a genotype expression reaches something in one and
nothing in the other.
--filter-expression and --filter-name are read in step, and the expressions are a REAL
literal comparison and a bare name, which are the two paths through commons-jexl's
arithmetic that SelectVariants' array already measures.
--mask takes the corpus's BED and its indexed VCF, because the tool reads a feature file of
either kind and asks it only where its features are.
--apply-allele-specific-filters is held at FALSE, and that is a claim about the PORT rather
than about the tool: with it on, the reference writes an AS_FilterStatus VALUE per allele
and applies the site filter name beside the mask one, and this port writes neither. The
one row that carried it diverged in exactly that way, which is how the gap was found.
--input and --read-index are held out: this tool reads no reads.
--add-output-vcf-command-line and --create-output-variant-index are held at FALSE for the
reason every variant writer holds them: one writes the run's own time into the header and
the other writes the output file's last-modified time into an index.
The read walkers' corpus, and the tool's own three knobs beside it. --minimum-base-quality
is the COLLECTOR's threshold rather than a read filter, so a base below it is dropped from
the counts while its read stays in the pileup: the two values are the default and one high
enough to empty every count.
--max-depth-per-sample is held at zero for the reason CheckPileup holds it: this port's
locus iterator has no downsampler, and a positive value is refused rather than answered
(gatk-rs#1102).
--intervals carries the window the reads are in and one they are not, which is the
difference between a table of rows and a table of none.
tumor_normal.bam, which is ONE file carrying two samples: the split this tool makes is by
sample name and not by input, so a tumour and a normal in one BAM is the shape a single
--input reads. Twelve reads of forty bases, all at chr1:101, because Mutect2's chain
refuses a read shorter than thirty and a locus the normal does not reach has no alternate.
--normal-sample names the sample that is the normal, and the two values are the two
samples: with `normal` the alternate is rare enough in the normal to be an artefact and a
row is written, and with `tumor` it is two reads of six, which is over the germline
threshold of a fifth, so the locus is dropped and the table is a header alone.
--error-prob moves the keep probability and nothing else, which is the column it writes.
--intervals keeps the shared window off the reads as its second value: a run that reaches
no locus draws no number at all, and the generator is shared across the whole traversal.
--max-depth-per-sample is held at zero for the reason CheckPileup holds it (gatk-rs#1102):
this port does not reproduce the downsampler's own random stream.
truth.vcf and calls.vcf, a pair built so that every one of the five concordance states
happens once: a call that agrees, a call with another alternate at a truth locus, a
FILTERED call at a truth locus, a truth record called nowhere, a filtered call away from
truth, and an unfiltered one. Without the last two the filter analysis has nothing to
count, and without the second the false positive and the false negative never coincide.
The filtered true negative carries TWO filters, so neither is unique to it: the
filter-analysis table counts uniqueness per RECORD rather than per filter.
The three annotated VCFs each carry two paths, because the file a state reaches is the
tool's own decision: a true positive is written to two of them, with the TRUTH record in
one and the EVAL record in the other.
--add-output-vcf-command-line and --create-output-variant-index are held at FALSE, as on
every other variant writer: one carries the run's clock and the other the output's
last-modified time.
duo.vcf is the driving callset and population.vcf the supporting one: the corpus already
carries a two-sample VCF and a panel with allele counts, which is exactly the pair this
tool was written for.
--num-reference-samples-if-no-call carries zero and a hundred. It is the argument that
decides what a site the panel does not carry gets: with zero and fewer than ten input
samples the prior is FLAT, so PP equals PL and PG is all zeros, and with a hundred it is a
pseudocount of two hundred reference chromosomes.
--default-to-allele-count and --discovered-allele-count-priors-off move where the counts
come from: AC rather than MLEAC, and the input's own samples in or out.
--pedigree is held out and --skip-family-priors is held TRUE: the family half is a second
algorithm this port does not carry, and every row that asked for it would measure that
refusal rather than the posteriors.
--add-output-vcf-command-line and --create-output-variant-index are held at false, as on
every other variant writer here.
somatic.vcf against tumor_normal.bam: the discovery calls are at the two sites that BAM
carries an alternate at, and a third call carries no AD at all, which is the SKIPPED
judgment and the only one a callset without depths can produce.
--discovery-sample-name, --val-case-sample-name and --val-control-sample-name are the
three names the tool reads, and they are the corpus's own: the VCF's sample is `tumor`
and the BAM's two are `tumor` and `normal`. A name nothing carries leaves both pileups
empty, which is a different answer rather than a refusal.
--min-power and --max-validation-normal-count carry the defaults and a value either side
of them: the first decides whether an unvalidated call counted as powered, the second
whether the normal's own alternate reads make it an artefact.
--annotated-vcf and --summary each carry two paths, because the three files this tool can
write are the three answers it gives.
pairs.bam, whose reads are PAIRED: the discordant-pair and split-read evidence both need
a mate, and the corpus's plain reads.bam has none.
Every output name carries the extension its writer tests for, and ONE of them carries a
name that does not: each of the four writers refuses a file it could not read back, before
the traversal, and `--sd-file` is where that refusal is measured. Giving every argument a
bad value would have refused every row; giving none would have measured none.
Every accepted name is plain `.txt`, so the claim excludes block-compressed (`.txt.gz`)
and `.bci` outputs: the port refuses both as its own limitation, and no row measures them.
--site-depth-locs-vcf carries the corpus's indexed VCF, whose records are biallelic SNVs:
the site-depth walk keeps those and steps past everything else.
--depth-evidence-intervals carries the corpus's BED, because the depth counts are per
interval and an interval file with no intervals is its own refusal.
--site-depth-min-mapq and --depth-evidence-min-mapq carry their two different defaults and
a value above them: the three floors are what let one read be counted for depth and not
for site depth.
--sequence-dictionary is pinned to the one that AGREES with the reads. The site-depth
writer asserts that the dictionary it was given and the BAM's are the same object, and
the corpus's other dictionary makes that an AssertionError rather than a user error.
sv.counts.tsv is the table the REFERENCE's own CollectReadCounts wrote, under the name
the codec recognises: `SimpleCountCodec.canDecode` tests for the extension `.counts.tsv`,
and the corpus's own `counts.tsv` does not have it, so it is the second value and the
no-suitable-codec refusal. A `.counts.tsv` carries its own SAM header, so the run never
consults --sequence-dictionary.
--input and --read-index are held out: this tool reads a feature file and no reads, and
the shared values pair a BAM index with a text table, which every row died on.
--output-prefix carries a directory prefix and the empty default, because the names this
tool chooses are the prefix and the sample glued together: with no prefix the files land
in the working directory, which the harness compares as the output.
--output-file-list carries a path and nothing: the file is written and closed BEFORE a
single record, so it exists even for a run that refuses.
--intervals and --exclude-intervals are held OUT. A feature file needs an index for a
bounded traversal and a text counts table has none, so every row that carried one measured
the random-access refusal rather than the rewrite.
counts.tsv, written by the REFERENCE's own CollectReadCounts: this tool is the next link
of that chain and reads exactly what it wrote.
--count-panel-of-normals and --annotated-intervals are held OUT. The first is an HDF5
panel and the second turns on the GC-bias correction; neither is written by this port, so
a row carrying either would measure the refusal rather than the standardisation.
--number-of-eigensamples is held out with them: it only means anything with a panel.
The two outputs carry two paths each, and a run with no panel writes the SAME bytes to
both: the denoised result is the standardised one when there is nothing to denoise with.
A SMALL window, chr1:101-200, because every base of the interval is a row whether a read
reaches it or not: the corpus's usual chr1:1-6000 would make a corpus file of six thousand
rows per accepted row of the array.
The three table omissions are held at TRUE. The files they would write carry quantiles
computed in a partitioned data store this port does not carry, so the port refuses a run
that asks for them; holding them true is what makes the array measure the per-base table
rather than that refusal, and it narrows the claim to exactly that file.
--output-format is held at CSV and --partition-type at `sample` for the same reason: the
other format is a padded table and the other partitions are the read group, the library
and the centre, none of which this port writes.
--calculate-coverage-over-genes is held out: it writes a per-gene table that is not
written here either.
--min-base-quality and --max-base-quality carry values INSIDE the byte range. Outside it
the parser refuses two different ways, which the tool's own golden measures.
--include-deletions is held at FALSE: it adds a sixth column, D, to every base-count
field, and the ported counter has the five bases and no deletion slot, so the port refuses
the run rather than writing a table a column short.
--start, --stop and --nBins carry values inside their declared ranges, and
--exclude-intervals a window OFF the reads as well as one inside them. The generator steps
each numeric argument below its minimum and the shared exclusion covers the whole window,
so twenty-two of twenty-three rows measured a parser refusal rather than the counting.
recal.table and recal2.table, both written by the REFERENCE's own BaseRecalibrator over
the corpus's two BAMs: the gather's input is another tool's output, which is what makes
this the third chain in the corpus.
Each row gathers ONE report, because a covering array assigns one value per argument and
--input is the only source. That is not a gather of nothing: the reduce still recomputes
the empirical qualities and the quantization at the first report's level count, so a
single-report row measures everything but the sum. The sum itself is measured by the
gather suite's golden, which carries the two-shard case.

constraints.why: A depth of one cannot be thinned, so this pair measures the argument without observing it.
No read of the corpus lies in that window, so the pileup is empty whatever the target is.
The master dictionary carries chrOther alone, so every interval over chr1 is refused before the traversal.
The reference carries chrOther alone, which the locus walker refuses for the same reason.
Inverted, it keeps only the non-primary reads, and the corpus has none: the pileup is empty.
A filter both enabled and disabled is refused by the descriptor before the tool runs.
One name for two files is the count refusal, which a row with the files the other way round measures already.
Two names for one file is the count refusal again, and every row carrying it measured nothing else.
A file where --split-output wants a directory is refused before any record; the rows it took were the ones that should vary the strata.
One writer on a directory is refused by htsjdk when it opens, before any record.
--split-output without a prefix is refused before any record.
sv_overlap.tsv names the SD track, which RM alone does not register.

exclude.--help: prints the usage and returns; the row would measure the argument parser rather than the tool
exclude.--version: prints the version and returns, same reason
exclude.--QUIET: suppresses the log on stderr, and what is compared is stdout and the output file
exclude.--verbosity: log level on stderr, same reason
exclude.--use-jdk-inflater: chooses an inflater, and the input is read the same way either way
exclude.--gcs-max-retries: reaches nothing without a cloud path in the row
exclude.--gcs-project-for-requester-pays: reaches nothing without a cloud path in the row
exclude.--gatk-config-file: a configuration file the corpus does not carry; varying it would measure the config loader
exclude.--arguments_file: expands into the command line itself, which is measured by the barclay-arguments-file suite instead
exclude.--quantize-quals: mutually exclusive with BOTH static-quantized-quals and round-down-quantized, and a covering array assigns every argument in every row: Barclay's mutex fires on an argument being SET, so even --round-down-quantized false refuses the row. Holding this one at its default is what lets the other two be varied, which is two covered arguments rather than one. The mutex message is measured by the mutex-target-names suite
exclude.--metadata: a feature source the Pileup runner does not open: it refuses the argument rather than answering without the column it asks for, so a row carrying one would measure the refusal
exclude.--mappability-track: a feature file the AnnotateIntervals runner does not open: it refuses the argument rather than writing a table without the column it asks for, so a row carrying one measures the refusal
exclude.--segmental-duplication-track: a feature file the AnnotateIntervals runner does not open: it refuses the argument rather than writing a table without the column it asks for, so a row carrying one measures the refusal
